**Saturday, June 23, 1956**

On the exact day you were born, Gamal Abdel Nasser was confirmed as president of Egypt in a national referendum. He was thirty-eight years old, a former army colonel who had overthrown the monarchy four years earlier, and he was about to make a move that would reshape the Middle East for generations. Six weeks after your birth — on July 26, 1956 — Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal, the waterway through which a significant portion of the world's oil flowed, and triggered a crisis that exposed, in public, how far Britain and France had fallen from imperial power. When the United States forced them to withdraw their invasion, the old European order understood something it had not yet fully admitted: the world had new masters. The child born on June 23 arrived on the first day of a new Middle Eastern era.

Six days after your birth — on June 29, 1956 — President Eisenhower signed the Federal Aid Highway Act, authorizing 41,000 miles of interstate highways. It was the largest public works project in American history. You grew up in the country that system created: suburban, automobile-dependent, the landscape of exit ramps and malls and commutes that became the defining American built environment for the rest of the century. The baby who arrived that Saturday was born into one America and watched another get paved into existence around her.

The summer of 1956 was also the summer rock and roll stopped being a subculture and became a force. By the time you arrived in June, "Heartbreak Hotel" had already spent eight weeks at number one. That September, Elvis appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show — filmed from the waist up, famously, because his hips were considered too dangerous for television. The child born in June 1956 grew up with rock and roll not as nostalgia or history, but as whatever was playing on the radio right now.

Four months after your birth, Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest. Hungary had risen in popular revolution against its Soviet-aligned government; for a few days it seemed they might succeed. The tanks ended that. Thousands died. Hundreds of thousands fled. The baby born in June 1956 grew up in a world where the Soviet capacity for violence was not theoretical. The Cold War was not abstract. It was Budapest in November.

Now here are two dates that landed on your exact birthday — one in your adolescence, one in your seventh decade.

**June 23, 1972** — your sixteenth birthday — President Nixon signed Title IX of the Education Amendments, a thirty-seven-word law prohibiting sex discrimination in any educational program receiving federal funding. It took years to fully implement and decades to fully contest, but it was the legal hinge that opened organized athletics, professional schools, and scientific training to women on terms the country had never before offered. You were sixteen years old on the day the law changed.

**June 23, 2016** — your sixtieth birthday — the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union. The Brexit referendum passed 52% to 48%. The European project that had built itself across your lifetime — constructed on the ruins of the war that predated your birth — began, that evening, to fracture in a new way. You were sixty years old on the day the result came in.

Step back and consider the arc. You were born into a world of roughly 2.8 billion people; there are now more than eight billion. You were born before Sputnik (October 1957), before the first human in space (1961), before the Moon landing (1969). The Polio vaccine was barely a year old. Segregation was the law in seventeen American states, and the Montgomery Bus Boycott — Rosa Parks had refused to move eight months before your birth — was still ongoing. The word "nuclear" carried a physical dread that later generations have inherited mostly as abstraction.

In 70 years, you have watched that world remake itself so completely that anyone transported from June 23, 1956 to this morning would need time simply to understand what planet they had arrived on. Born the day an Egyptian colonel became president and set the old empires reeling, you have had a front-row seat to everything that followed — the highways and the rock and roll and the Cold War's long tension and its eventual implosion, the legal revolutions and the democratic shocks, and now a world in which machines can read, write, and reason in ways that would have seemed like science fiction to anyone alive on the Saturday you were born.
